section_summary: This section documents exchange controls imposed by Japanese authorities in China and Japan, their effects on American exporters, and U.S. diplomatic protests. It also includes reports on Japanese currency, gold reserves and trade, correspondence about blocked American funds, and the opening pages of a study of American companies’ finances in Japan.

people.name: M. Rothschild
people.role: Manager of the Rieser Company’s Chefoo branch

people.name: Maxwell M. Hamilton
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: O. R. Johnson
people.role: Assistant Treasurer, Bates International Bag Company

people.name: Harry I. T. Creswell
people.role: Lieutenant Colonel and Acting General Staff Military Attaché

subfiles.title: Export Subjected to Controlled Exchange
subfiles.about: Chinese National Government regulations require exporters of listed commodities to book exchange through designated banks.
subfiles.summary: The article describes the proposed controls, possible enforcement in Shanghai, and exporters’ concern about losses on contracts already booked through foreign banks.

subfiles.title: Exchange Control in North China
subfiles.about: Sokobin forwards a newspaper version of a Domei report on North China exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the July 29 report as possibly of interest.

subfiles.title: North China Restriction on Foreign Trade
subfiles.about: Authorities plan import and export licensing and barter arrangements in North China.
subfiles.summary: Reports plans to link imports with exports and increase foreign currency held by the Federal Reserve Bank of China.

subfiles.title: Singer Sewing Machine Company exchange difficulties
subfiles.about: Points to a letter requesting help with exchange controls affecting Singer’s Japanese branch.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references the company’s letter and enclosed memorandum.

subfiles.title: Peanut oil exports by Mitsui
subfiles.about: A Japanese firm ships peanut oil at market exchange rates while non-Japanese firms face official rates.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin reports discriminatory exchange treatment in a 1,200-ton shipment.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Sokobin’s peanut oil telegram
subfiles.about: Restates the report that exchange rules favor Japanese peanut oil exporters.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrases Sokobin’s September 20 telegram.

subfiles.title: Possible undervaluation of exports
subfiles.to: American Consul at Tsingtao; Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Johnson asks whether the peanut oil shipments should be reported as undervalued or subsidized.
subfiles.summary: Asks whether Section 682 of the Consular Regulations applies.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Johnson’s undervaluation inquiry
subfiles.to: American Consul at Tsingtao; Department of State
subfiles.about: Restates Johnson’s question about reporting Japanese shipments as undervalued or subsidized.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrases the September 24 telegram.

subfiles.title: Possible yen peg to the dollar
subfiles.about: Japan is considering shifting the yen’s peg from sterling to the U.S. dollar.
subfiles.summary: Grew says a change depends on developments in Europe.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of yen peg telegram
subfiles.about: Restates the confidential report on a possible yen peg to the U.S. dollar.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrases Grew’s September 27 report.

subfiles.title: Exchange control regulations
subfiles.about: Cross-references a telegram on controls channeling goods and the legal treatment of Japan and yen.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the cited regulations exempt Japan and yen from foreign-country and foreign-currency definitions.

subfiles.title: Circulation of Japanese Fiduciary Currency in Hong Kong
subfiles.about: The report examines discounted Japanese notes circulating in Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Donovan compares a press account with bankers’ information. He reports that notes issued for Japanese troops in occupied China were traded privately at a steep discount in Hong Kong, sometimes smuggled into Japan, and sometimes refused there. Banks could not reliably distinguish the special notes from ordinary yen.

subfiles.title: Japanese Restrictions of Export Trade at Tsingtao
subfiles.about: Sokobin describes Japanese export permits and exchange rules that disadvantage American traders at Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: The despatch recounts Japanese attempts to direct exporters to Japanese banks, the American protest, and a discussion with the Japanese Consul General. Sokobin argues that official exchange rates make American exports commercially impossible while Japanese firms continue shipping. He frames the issue as interference with treaty rights and encloses a protest letter, conversation memorandum, and price calculation.

subfiles.title: Protest against interference with American exporters
subfiles.about: Sokobin rejects Japanese authority over American export and exchange operations at Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: Invokes U.S.–China treaty rights and protests interference.

subfiles.title: Conversation with the Japanese Consul General
subfiles.about: Sokobin records a dispute with S. Ohtaka over treaty rights, trade freedom, and exchange rates.
subfiles.summary: Ohtaka argues that the North China regime need not honor earlier Chinese treaties and that exchange differences harm Japanese merchants. Sokobin rejects Japanese interference with American exporters. Ohtaka suggests a future system linking imports and exports.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Prices
subfiles.about: A calculation questions whether Mitsubishi’s peanut oil exports used the official yen rate.
subfiles.summary: Estimates large apparent losses on two shipments if valued at that rate.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum on Japan’s gold and exchange position
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential analysis of Japan’s gold and foreign exchange position.
subfiles.summary: Recommends that the Secretary read the attached analysis.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold and Foreign Exchange Position, August 1 to October 27, 1938
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses Japanese gold exports, dollar assets, and trade balances.
subfiles.summary: The analysis estimates that much exported gold remained earmarked in the United States, limiting the net decline in Japan’s monetary gold stock. It notes the sharp fall in Japanese banks’ short-term dollar assets and warns that earmarked gold may soon be needed. Its trade analysis adjusts for transactions within the yen bloc and considers whether reduced imports can be sustained without weakening exports.

subfiles.title: Universal Leaf Tobacco exchange requirement
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report that Universal Leaf Tobacco faced a discriminatory exchange purchase requirement.
subfiles.summary: Notes a suggested protest through the Embassy in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Japanese mink skins shipped through China
subfiles.about: Cross-references a suspected attempt to avoid Japan’s export exchange rules.
subfiles.summary: Notes that mink skins sent through Shanghai were redirected to New York.

subfiles.title: Exchange control and soda ash imports
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on exchange controls limiting soda ash imports for Japanese bottle production.
subfiles.summary: Notes resulting beer business and a comment attributed to Leith-Ross.

subfiles.title: Currency difficulties at Chefoo
subfiles.about: Rieser describes banking and currency obstacles to his company’s Chefoo trade.
subfiles.summary: He reports costly Shanghai drafts, Japanese restrictions, and workers’ refusal of the new currency.

subfiles.title: Reply to Rieser on Chefoo currency
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Rieser’s account of Chefoo’s currency situation.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Rieser for the information and his comments on foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Bates International Bag Company blocked royalties
subfiles.about: Bates asks for help remitting royalties owed by its Japanese subsidiary.
subfiles.summary: The company says Japanese exchange restrictions have blocked payment of about ¥200,000 and asks what steps might secure payment.

subfiles.title: Instruction to inquire about Bates remittance
subfiles.about: The Embassy is asked to raise Bates’s delayed remittance permit informally.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Bates’s letter and requests an inquiry with Japanese exchange authorities.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bates International Bag Company
subfiles.about: The Department tells Bates it has asked the Tokyo Embassy to inquire about the blocked funds.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the ¥200,000 claim and reports the Embassy referral.

subfiles.title: Government Control of Exchange
subfiles.about: The report describes Japanese rules intended to curb currency arbitrage through China.
subfiles.summary: It explains how traders profited by buying Chinese yuan and converting them to yen, then lists new licensing, remittance, and customs reporting requirements. The report says Japanese authorities sought to close this route and protect the yen.

subfiles.title: Possible yen devaluation
subfiles.about: Cross-references a conversation in which the Swedish Consul mentioned possible yen devaluation.
subfiles.summary: Notes Gaston’s account of Japanese negotiators discussing devaluation.

subfiles.title: Reported yen stabilization at twenty cents
subfiles.about: Cross-references an American merchant’s report of yen stabilization at twenty U.S. cents.
subfiles.summary: Records the reported exchange rate.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file enclosure
subfiles.about: Records administrative charges and routing of a file enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Lists clerks, dates, and file references.

subfiles.title: Rieser Company inquiry about Chefoo exchange
subfiles.about: Rieser asks how Japanese currency measures will affect his Chefoo business.
subfiles.summary: He compares exchange rates with Swatow and reports that workers reject the Japanese-backed currency.

subfiles.title: Department reply on Chefoo restrictions
subfiles.about: The Department explains its representations concerning Chefoo export and currency restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton describes the planned transition between Chinese and Federal Reserve Bank notes and ongoing representations to Japan. He reports that Chefoo authorities began allowing some existing export commitments without requiring exchange sales at the pegged rate.

subfiles.title: Settlement of blocked cotton payments
subfiles.about: The American Cotton Cooperative Association reports that Japanese cotton payments have been settled.
subfiles.summary: Thanks the Department for its efforts after the delayed amounts were liquidated.

subfiles.title: Tobacco shipments held at Tsingtao
subfiles.about: Japanese authorities hold Yee Tsoong Tobacco Company shipments, possibly over exchange rules.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin reports the hold and asks about an Embassy letter to Universal Leaf Tobacco.

subfiles.title: Rieser follow-up on Chefoo currency restrictions
subfiles.about: Rieser says Japanese currency restrictions now affect old as well as new Chefoo orders.
subfiles.summary: He asks what course the firm should take, noting workers’ refusal of the new currency and concern that shipments must settle through the Yokohama Specie Bank.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Rieser’s follow-up
subfiles.about: Hamilton clarifies the distinction between local note circulation and foreign exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: He says the March 10 date concerns local use of notes, leaves the firm’s business decision to Rieser, and confirms continued efforts to remove the restrictions.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs routing notation
subfiles.about: A largely illegible note appears to concern distribution of a document.
subfiles.summary: Brief handwritten or stamped routing notation.

subfiles.title: The Fiscal Position of American Companies in Japan at the Beginning of 1939
subfiles.about: The report surveys American companies’ liquid assets and exchange difficulties in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The opening sections examine Standard-Vacuum, Goodrich, Victor, Ford, direct exporters, retiring Americans, IBM, and motion picture companies. They describe blocked royalties and dividends, delayed permits, forward exchange contracts, payment in goods, and efforts to protect dollar proceeds. The report continues beyond page 320.
